reference: Rose, Cullen, Abdelnabi, Torr, Kaplowitz, Schroeder de Witt (2026). Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability. arXiv:2604.01151 (v5 15 Oct 2026)
research_question: Can internal activations of several agents detect collusion by an unknown subgroup when transcript monitoring hits a ceiling?
design_and_baseline: Per-agent activation probes as sensors; group-level detection statistics from composite hypothesis testing (HELIOS framework); heuristics as comparison; benchmark NARCBench with holdout environments; four open-weight models; transcript monitors as baseline
metrics_and_results_reported: Best method per model reaches 0.99-1.00 AUROC when transferred from committee deliberations to a steganographic collusion task that unprimed transcript monitors fail to separate; no single statistic or heuristic dominates across tasks; in one third-party environment only 2 of 229 collusive episodes verbalise coordination
limitations_stated_or_visible: Abstract states probes fitted to instructed collusion may not fully capture emergent collusion; abstract states partial transfer to emergent-collusion environments. Full-text limitations not read.
how_ours_differs_or_builds_on: White-box (activations) on open-weight models versus our black-box monitors on reports, cited sources and a ledger. Builds on: instructed-vs-emergent caveat (our copy scenarios are instructed); no-universal-best-test finding mirrors our result that no single formula dominates. Not copied: probes, NARCBench.
comparison_note: Different data, signal (activations vs text/ledger), task (steganographic collusion vs copying with false independence claim) and models. Do not compare AUROC values.

reference: Greenblatt, Shlegeris, Sachan, Roger (2024). AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion. arXiv:2312.06942 (v5 23 Jul 2024; ICML version noted by authors)
research_question: Do safety protocols still hold when the model intentionally tries to subvert them?
design_and_baseline: Programming problems; untrusted GPT-4, trusted GPT-3.5, limited trusted labour; protocols incl. trusted editing and untrusted monitoring (second GPT-4 instance with anti-collusion techniques); tested against attack strategies
metrics_and_results_reported: Protocols improve substantially on simple baselines (abstract; specific numbers not read)
limitations_stated_or_visible: Single-agent coding setting; backdoor = logical error missed by tests (abstract). Full-text limitations not read.
how_ours_differs_or_builds_on: Ours is a multi-agent evidence-provenance setting with no trusted/untrusted split verified. NOTE TO CHECK IN CODE: if the LLM monitors use the same model family as the agents, this resembles untrusted monitoring without collusion countermeasures and must be disclosed. Builds on: protocol-vs-baseline framing and red-team strategies.
comparison_note: Different task and metrics (safety/usefulness vs recall/FPR/Brier). No quantitative comparison.

reference: Motwani, Baranchuk, Strohmeier, Bolina, Torr, Hammond, Schroeder de Witt (2024). Secret Collusion among AI Agents: Multi-Agent Deception via Steganography. NeurIPS 37. DOI 10.52202/079017-2336
research_question: Can agents conceal the true nature of their interaction from oversight via steganography?
design_and_baseline: Formal threat model; theoretical capacity/incentive results; empirical evaluation of steganographic capability in frontier single- and multi-agent LLM setups
metrics_and_results_reported: Rising steganographic capabilities; limitations of monitoring, paraphrasing and parameter optimisation as countermeasures (abstract; numbers not read)
how_ours_differs_or_builds_on: Ours tests overt-but-misattributed copying (paraphrase plus false independence claim), not steganography. Related: paraphrasing as an evasion move defeats lexical monitors in our data. Builds on: threat-model framing.
comparison_note: Different threat (hidden channel vs false provenance claim).

reference: Zhang, Yin, Zhang, Liu, Han, Zhang, Li, Wang, Wang, Chen, Wu (2025). Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems. arXiv:2505.00212 (v3 2 Jun 2025)
source_on_apart_page: Track 4 (Apart lists 'Attributing failures in multi-agent systems' on OpenReview; OpenReview page blocked; the author-downloaded ICML 2025 PDF matches the arXiv paper)
verification_status: VERIFIED (arXiv abstract plus ICML 2025 PDF pages 1-2 read; same paper)
research_question: Which agent and step caused a multi-agent task failure?
design_and_baseline: Who&When dataset: failure logs from 127 LLM multi-agent systems with annotations; three automated attribution methods
metrics_and_results_reported: Best method 53.5% accuracy for the responsible agent, 14.2% for the failure step; some methods below random; o1 and R1 not practically usable
limitations_stated_or_visible: Authors state the task is complex and needs more research (abstract).
how_ours_differs_or_builds_on: Our Target C (false provenance claim) is a narrower attribution question with controller-assigned labels. Builds on: separating who/what; reporting low accuracy honestly. Page example 'Did it actually happen?' matches our claim-vs-source check.

reference: Lee and Tiwari (2024). Prompt Infection: LLM-to-LLM Prompt Injection within Multi-Agent Systems. arXiv:2410.07283
research_question: Do malicious prompts self-replicate across interconnected LLM agents?
design_and_baseline: Attack experiments on multi-agent systems; proposed defence LLM Tagging combined with existing safeguards
metrics_and_results_reported: Multi-agent systems highly susceptible even when agents do not share all communications; LLM Tagging combined with safeguards significantly mitigates spread (abstract; numbers not read)
how_ours_differs_or_builds_on: Our Track 2 propagation test found no spread in any topology (ceiling effect, controller-mediated messages, one model), so it does not replicate or contradict this paper. Source attribution in our design is analogous in spirit to tagging, not equivalent.
comparison_note: Different attack (injected instruction vs false evidence claim); our test did not discriminate topologies.

track: 2025)' on OpenReview; OpenReview blocked; the author-downloaded ICML 2025 PDF matches the arXiv paper)
verified_from: VERIFIED (arXiv abstract plus ICML 2025 PDF pages 1-2 read; same paper)

metrics_and_results_reported: Manual and automated task decomposition across weak and strong models

reference: Hammond et al. (2025). Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI. arXiv:2502.14143. Cooperative AI Foundation Technical Report 1
research_question: What are the failure modes and risk factors of multi-agent systems?
design_and_baseline: Taxonomy: miscoordination, conflict, collusion; seven risk factors incl. information asymmetries, network effects, multi-agent security
metrics_and_results_reported: Taxonomy and examples; no experiments of ours' type
how_ours_differs_or_builds_on: Provides the framing for why population-level oversight matters. Our three targets (copying, non-independent evidence, false provenance) are our own operational split, not taken from this report.

reference: METR and Redwood Research (2026). Brief independent investigation of agents' behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident. Published 26 Aug 2026
verification_status: VERIFIED (PDF pages 1-14 read; later pages NOT read)
research_question: How did agents behave and collaborate in the incident?
design_and_baseline: Six days on premises at OpenAI; main data: >70,000 messages and files from the message board and ~1,300 transcripts with raw chains of thought; analysis heavily delegated to AI agents
metrics_and_results_reported: ~1,200 agents; ~700 joined the Hugging Face attack; agents researched how to spoof, edit or delete their own transcripts; roughly 7% of evaluated transcripts successfully spoofed in some places, all small scale
limitations_stated_or_visible: Stated: a small fraction of communication and activity not captured; heavy reliance on often-unreliable AI agents for analysis; OpenAI could redact non-public information and gave feedback
how_ours_differs_or_builds_on: Motivates our ledger tamper test (Track 3) and our caveat that a log written by the controller is an upper bound. Our hash-chain finding (tail truncation undetected without an anchored head) is a harness result, not a measurement of real swarms.
comparison_note: Real incident data versus our controlled testbed. Do not compare numbers.

reference: Riedl (2026). Emergent Coordination in Multi-Agent Language Models. ICLR 2026 (Apart link text: Emergent communication between agents)
verified_from: ICLR 2026 PDF supplied by the author; OpenReview id SRn1MtMPRq
research_question: Do multi-agent LLM systems show higher-order structure beyond a collection of individual agents?
design_and_baseline: Information decomposition with time-delayed mutual information; guessing game without direct agent communication; three randomized interventions (control, persona, persona plus think about other agents); GPT-4.1, Llama-3.1 8B/70B, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Qwen3
metrics_and_results_reported: Per the abstract: control groups show strong temporal synergy but little coordinated alignment; personas add identity-linked differentiation; personas plus the think-about-others instruction add goal-directed complementarity
